In addition to sealing, insulating ducts can help reduce heat loss. Duct insulation is typically applied by wrapping fiberglass insulation around the ducts. Other products, such as spray foam, can also be used to insulate ducts, depending on the application and installation requirements. If insulation is poor, the existing wraps are often replaced with more effective material. ENERGY STAR® (ENERGY STAR, 2025) recommends insulating ducts in unconditioned areas (such as attics, crawlspaces, and garages) with insulation that has an R-value of R-6 or higher. The National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) Standard Work Specifications require insulating all ducts outside the thermal boundary to a minimum of R-8, and insulating all ducts exposed to the exterior to a minimum of R-12 (NREL, 2025). However, in contrast to ducts located in attics, crawlspaces, or garages, insulating ducts that run within enclosed building envelope cavities— such as wall or floor assemblies—can be more challenging. This type of insulation is typically performed as part of broader envelope insulation work. 1.2 Technical Measure Details HVAC duct insulation requirements depend on duct location and climate zone. According to IECC 2015, supply and return air ducts must be insulated with at least R-6 insulation when located in unconditioned spaces, at least R-8 insulation when located outside the building in climate zones 1 through 4, and a minimum of R-12 insulation in climate zones 5 through 8. 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. When located within a building envelope assembly, the duct must be separated from the building exterior or unconditioned or exempt spaces by a minimum of R-8 insulation in climate zones 1 through 4, and a minimum of R-12 insulation in climate zones 5 through 8 (IECC, 2015). After ductwork improvements, duct insulation can vary based on the duct location within a home. However, for modeling purposes, ResStock assumes uniform duct insulation throughout the entire dwelling unit. After improving insulation on HVAC ducts, the final R-value can range from R-4.2 to R-12, depending on factors such as climate, duct placement, and overall system design. According to research by NLR, increasing duct insulation to R-8 is considered a reasonable target (Andrews, 2001). This measure assumes insulation is added only to ducts located in unconditioned spaces, wherever accessible (e.g., attics, crawlspaces, or garages). If the ducts are currently uninsulated, they are wrapped with R-12 insulation, such as flexible fiberglass duct wrap or pre-formed insulation. Since IECC requires a minimum of R-6 insulation for ducts in unconditioned spaces (IECC, 2015), ducts that already meet or exceed this standard are not upgraded. Therefore, if the existing insulation is below R-6, the old wrap is removed and replaced with high-performance R- 12 insulation. Ducts integrated with the building envelope are not modified.
